segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the last Tuesday in October, Mr Silas Rowe let his scholars out of the east wing of Amberlight House at four, because by half past there was no reading to be had without candles, and candles came out of the eighty pounds a year he was paid to be curate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He counted them through the yard gate as he always did, twenty-six of them, the Ludd boy last and sideways. Then he turned back for his hat, and stopped in the middle of the yard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The main block of the house had been shut since old Sir Edward Marchmont died in the spring of 1812. Its windows were shuttered, as they had been every day Mr Rowe had crossed that yard. Behind the second shutter from the corner, a thin seam of candlelight moved from left to right, paused, and went up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stood until it had gone altogether. Then he walked home by the churchyard wall and told his wife, and by nine the next morning he was telling the draper's counter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Hale, who keeps the circulating library above the draper's shop and the draper's counter below it, had the matter ready before he had finished.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: Mr Harker. Edward Harker. He came Friday on the coach with two boxes and a man, and he has the main rooms by the Marchmont family's leave, which is all the Marchmont family have ever done for this parish, for they have never once set foot in it. He is trustee to a young lady. There is a bequest to her out of old Sir Edward's estate, and she is no relation to the name at all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Miss Phoebe Langton was at the end of the counter with four yards of black crape under her hand, waiting to be served, and her measuring tape round her wrist as it generally was. Mrs Hale turned, remembered her, and brought out a folded paper from beside the till.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: And this came down for you, my dear, by the same man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The note was six lines. Full mourning for a Miss Fairfax, made up and delivered within the week, nothing in it of trimming or of taste, and no name at the foot but two initials. Phoebe read it twice.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: He does not say what she is like. He does not say when I am to measure her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Honoria Pike had come in at the word mourning, as she generally did, and set her basket on the counter.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: A house does not light itself after six years dark, my dear, unless there is something in it the parish is not to have. Mourning within the week, and no measuring. Six years, and now candles.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: You will carry the order up yourself. And you will look sharp about you while you are in that hall.
